253.title: Where the gods hid
253.hook: the gods hide from Death inside one syllable; why Hindus begin with om
253.howItsDone: Om is chanted by Hindus at the start and end of prayers, recitations and many rituals; the Mandukya Upanishad, with Gaudapada's verse commentary (Karika), is a central text in Advaita Vedanta study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashvattha, and the end of the Katha: the heart's knots cut, and Nachiketa walked out of Death's house free.

An old Upanishad tells this story. The gods were afraid of Death. So they hid inside the Vedas, the sacred hymns, and wrapped themselves in the hymns' meters like a cloak. It didn't work. Death saw them there, the text says, the way you'd see a fish in water. So the gods rose up out of the hymns and slipped into one sound: om. The deathless, the story calls it. The fearless. And having entered it, the gods became deathless.
screen: `THE GODS HIDE FROM DEATH.` → `A FISH IN WATER.` → `SAFE INSIDE OM.`

segments.voice: Why would a sound be a hiding place? This week's Upanishad, the Mandukya, answers in its first line. Om. This syllable is all this. Everything that was, is and will be is om, and whatever is beyond time, that too is om. Not a symbol of all this. All this. In Sanskrit the word for syllable, akshara, also means the imperishable: what can't wear away. So the gods didn't hide in a word. They hid in the one thing that doesn't end. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: Brahman, the one reality under everything, can be met in a sound. It's why Hindus begin so many prayers with om. Om namah shivaya. Om gam ganapataye namah. A priest's first breath at a puja; a grandparent's first word at dawn. Om is chanted as three sounds, a, u and m, flowing into each other, and then a silence after. This week, the Mandukya maps those three sounds onto the three places you live every day: waking, dreaming and deep sleep. And the silence onto something it simply calls the fourth. Today, om is printed on yoga mats and played on meditation apps as a nice, calm hum. Hindus mean more by it. Saying om, the tradition says, isn't making a relaxing noise. It's saying the name of everything, and stepping, for one breath, into the sound the gods called deathless. Twelve verses. One syllable. All this.
screen: `OM: THIS SYLLABLE IS ALL THIS.` · `AKSHARA: SYLLABLE, AND THE IMPERISHABLE.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.` · then, large: `OM IS ALL THIS.`

segments.voice: If you're comfortable, chant om once, slowly, out loud or under your breath: let it rise out of silence, hum for a while, fade, and then stay in the silence after it. If chanting isn't for you, listen to any sound in the room the same way: where it starts, how long it lasts, where it goes. Each time, rest in the quiet that follows.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Twelve verses on om, the syllable that is all this: past, present, future, and what's beyond time.
Your line: om is all this. The gods hid in it, and it held. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.

254.title: Indra and the mirror
254.hook: Indra and a demon king learn the self from a pan of water; atman is not the body
254.carry: the self is not the body
254.howItsDone: 'Ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2) is taught in Hindu Vedanta as one of four mahavakyas, great sayings, each drawn from a different Veda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gods hid from Death inside om, and the Mandukya Upanishad began: om, this syllable is all this.

Another old story. Prajapati, the creator, announced: there is a self that never grows old, never dies, never grieves, never hungers. Whoever finds it wins everything. Two students came to learn it, firewood in hand, the old sign of a student. Indra, king of the gods. And Virochana, king of the demons. They served Prajapati for thirty-two years. Then he said: dress in your finest clothes and look into a pan of water. What do you see? Ourselves, sir, all dressed up, down to our hair and nails. That, said Prajapati, is the self. Both went home happy.
screen: `A SELF THAT NEVER DIES.` → `A PAN OF WATER.` → `THAT IS THE SELF?`

segments.voice: Virochana went home and taught the demons: the body is the self. Dress it, feed it, please it, and you win this world and the next. But Indra, on the road home, stopped. If the body is the self, then when the body is dressed up, the self is dressed up. When the body goes blind, the self goes blind. When the body dies, the self dies. That's no self that never dies. I see no good in this, he said, and turned around. Many teachers read Prajapati's answer as a test: the reflection was the easy answer, and only one student questioned it. That's the teaching, and one of Hinduism's biggest: atman, the self. You have a body, and you are more than it. The Mandukya's second verse says it plainly: all this is Brahman, and this self is Brahman. Ayam atma brahma, one of the four great sayings, the mahavakyas. Then it maps that self in four quarters. The first is vaishvanara, the waking self: knowing outward, enjoying solid things, food, faces, the chair under you. In om, it's the first sound, a. The Mandukya doesn't call waking life fake, or the body bad. Waking is a real quarter. Just not the whole. Today the pan of water is a phone. A person can spend an hour on one photo and feel their worth rise and fall with it. Hindu teaching doesn't say stop caring how you look. It says that face is where you live, not who you are. Indra stopped on the road. Anyone can.
screen: `VIROCHANA: THE BODY IS THE SELF.` · `INDRA TURNS BACK.` · `AYAM ATMA BRAHMA: THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.` · `THE FIRST QUARTER: WAKING.` · then, large: `MORE THAN THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Be fully in the waking state: your weight on the chair, the sounds around you, the air on your skin, the taste in your mouth. This is the first quarter, knowing outward. Then gently notice that you're aware of all of it, the body included: it's appearing to you. Ask Indra's question quietly, is this all of me, and rest there without answering.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The self is Brahman, and it has four quarters. The first is vaishvanara: the waking state, knowing outward.
Your line: the self is not the body. Indra turned back on the road; tomorrow, what Prajapati told him next.

255.title: Indra and the dream
255.hook: Indra's second try: the dreaming self, lit from within, still weeps
255.carry: the dreamer isn't the deepest self
255.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya and Gaudapada's Karika are studied together; the comparison between dreaming and waking is a classic subject of that study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Virochana took his reflection for the self, and Indra turned back. In the Mandukya Upanishad, the waking self is one quarter, not the whole.

Indra walked back to Prajapati, firewood in hand again, and said: the body can go blind, and die. That can't be the self. True, said Prajapati. Stay another thirty-two years. When the years were done, he gave a new answer. The one who moves about happily in dreams: that is the self. It made sense. A dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind, or lame when the body is lame. Indra set off home, pleased. And again, on the road, he stopped.
screen: `BACK AGAIN, FIREWOOD IN HAND.` → `THE DREAMER IS THE SELF?` → `AGAIN, HE STOPS.`

segments.voice: Because in a dream, Indra saw, the dreamer still suffers. It's as if it's being struck, as if it's being chased. It feels pain. It even weeps. That's no self beyond sorrow. He turned around a second time. The Mandukya gives this dreamer a beautiful name: taijasa, the shining one, from tejas, brilliance. Its fourth verse says the dream self knows inward and enjoys the subtle: images, memories, feelings, made of mind. Commentators explain the name. In a dream there's no sun and no lamp, and yet everything is seen. The dream is lit from within. In om, it's the second sound, u, between a and m, the way dreaming sits between waking and deep sleep. So the story and the verse agree. Dreaming is a real quarter of the self, a whole world made by the mind. And it still isn't the deepest self, because what's in it can frighten and grieve. That's the teaching. You are not only the one who acts by day, and not only the one who dreams by night. Many Hindu teachers name a witness of both, the sakshi, the one who sees, and the path is learning to stand there. Today, nobody has to be asleep to dream. A fight replayed at three in the morning. A worst case that hasn't happened. A feed that pulls you in. A world lit from within, and it feels completely real. Indra's question still works: is this the deepest me, or something I'm watching?
screen: `THE DREAMER STILL WEEPS.` · `TAIJASA: THE SHINING ONE.` · `U: BETWEEN WAKING AND SLEEP.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `IS THIS THE DEEPEST ME?`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let an image come, a place you love, a face, a color, and notice there's no outer light, yet you can see it: that's the shining one, lighting a world from inside. Let it fade and another come, and watch them the way you'd watch a dream, without getting pulled in. Then let them all go, and notice what was watching.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The second quarter is taijasa, the shining one: the dream state, knowing inward, lit from within.
Your line: the dreamer isn't the deepest self. Even the shining one can weep. Two hundred fifty-five days now.

256.title: Indra and deep sleep
256.hook: Indra's third try: dreamless sleep, and the bliss that wants nothing
256.carry: ananda: the peace that wants nothing
256.howItsDone: Some Vedanta teachers use the everyday report 'I slept well' as a starting point for reflecting on deep sleep as the Mandukya's third quarter, prajna.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: taijasa, the shining one, the dreamer. And Indra saw that even the dreamer weeps.

Thirty-two more years with Prajapati. Then a third answer. When someone is fast asleep, whole and at peace, and sees no dream: that is the self. Deathless. Fearless. Indra liked it. No pain there, no chasing, no tears. He started home. And for the third time, he stopped on the road. In deep sleep, he thought, nobody knows anything. Not 'this is me.' Not the beings around. It's as if the self has simply gone out. I see no good in this. He walked back.
screen: `A THIRD ANSWER.` → `FAST ASLEEP, NO DREAM.` → `HAS THE SELF GONE OUT?`

segments.voice: Here the Mandukya gives an answer Indra didn't have on the road. Its fifth verse: where the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream, that is deep sleep. And deep sleep isn't nothing. Its self is called prajna, the knowing one. It has become one, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss, enjoying bliss. Why a mass of knowing? In waking you know a world; in dream you know images. In deep sleep there's nothing to know, so the knowing isn't spread among things. It's gathered, like light with nothing to fall on. Commentators say that's why people wake up and say, I slept so well. Something was there to enjoy it. Verse six goes further: this quarter is the source and the end of beings. Shankara explains that waking and dream come out of it every morning and fold back into it every night. In om, it's m, the lips closing. So Indra was half right. Deep sleep isn't the final self, and he kept going, and so does the Mandukya. But it shows what Hindus call ananda, bliss: the deepest peace comes with no objects at all. No wanting. An older Upanishad says that in deep sleep a father is no longer a father, a thief no longer a thief. Today, rest gets sold as a product: the right app, the right pillow, one more purchase. The Mandukya points at what happens every night for free. When wanting stops, peace is already there. Many Vedanta teachers put it simply: that peace isn't made by things. It's what you are underneath them.
screen: `NO DESIRE, NO DREAM.` · `PRAJNA: A MASS OF KNOWING.` · `THE SOURCE OF WAKING AND DREAM.` · `ANANDA: PEACE WITH NOTHING IN IT.` · then, large: `PEACE ISN'T MADE BY THINGS.`

segments.voice: Let the body get heavy, as if drifting toward sleep, but stay just awake, wanting nothing from these minutes, letting images and thoughts pass without following them. See if you can taste a little of what the text describes: no wanting, nothing to hold, just a quiet, gathered knowing. Don't try to fall asleep; just rest near it.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The third quarter is prajna: deep sleep, no desire, no dream, a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.
Your line: ananda, the peace that wants nothing. Even dreamless sleep is full of it, the text says. Day two hundred fifty-six, done.

257.title: The hundred and one years
257.hook: Indra's last lesson after 101 years: the fourth, the awareness every state appears in
257.carry: turiya: the awareness under every state
257.tomorrow: The student who asked about om
257.howItsDone: Mandukya verse 7 is central to Advaita Vedanta, where 'the fourth' (turiya) names pure awareness; other Vedanta schools read the verse as describing the Lord beyond the three states.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: prajna, deep sleep, a mass of knowing, made of bliss. And Indra walked back a third time.

Prajapati told Indra: stay five more years. Thirty-two, thirty-two, thirty-two, five. One hundred and one years, the story says, Indra lived as a student, and he was the king of the gods. Then came the last teaching. This body is mortal, held by death. But it's the home of a self that has no body and doesn't die. The one who knows 'let me hear this' is the self; the ear is only for hearing. The one who knows 'let me think this' is the self; the mind is its divine eye.
screen: `101 YEARS A STUDENT.` → `THE BODY: A HOME.` → `THE ONE WHO KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Not the body, not the dreamer, not the sleeper. The knower behind all of them. The Mandukya's seventh verse names the same thing, almost entirely by what it isn't. Not knowing inward: that was dream. Not knowing outward: that was waking. Not a mass of knowing: that was deep sleep. Unseen. Ungraspable. Unthinkable. Unnameable. In it the world comes to rest. Peaceful, shanta. Auspicious, shiva. Not two, advaita. This, they consider the fourth. That is the self. The verse's own word is plain, caturtha, fourth; later tradition calls it turiya. And it isn't a fourth state, a place you travel to after sleep. Here's an image modern teachers use. Three films play on one screen: a busy city, a wild dream, a long black frame. The screen isn't any of them. It's what all three play on, and it never changes. On this reading, the fourth is the awareness that waking, dream and sleep come and go in, here right now under this moment. That's the heart of Shankara's school, Advaita Vedanta. Other Hindu schools read the verse as the Lord's own nature beyond the three states. Both agree you are more than any state you pass through. Today, a life has many films on its screen: the student, the daughter, the profile, the mood of the week. Each one feels like all of you while it plays. The fourth is the Hindu answer to who's watching. It took a king of the gods a hundred and one years. You get to hear it in five minutes, and spend a lifetime on it.
screen: `NOT INWARD, NOT OUTWARD.` · `PEACEFUL, AUSPICIOUS, NOT TWO.` · `THREE FILMS, ONE SCREEN.` · `NOT A STATE: WHAT STATES APPEAR IN.` · then, large: `TURIYA.`

segments.voice: Notice that you're awake, then notice the awareness that knows you're awake; the Mandukya's map says the same awareness was there in last night's dreams, and in the deep sleep after them. Rest in that awareness itself, not in anything it's aware of. When a thought or sound arrives, let it play on the screen, and stay with the screen.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Its seventh verse: the fourth, peaceful, auspicious, not two. Not another state, but what all three appear in.
Your line: turiya, the awareness under every state. The films keep changing; the screen stays. Until tomorrow.

258.title: The student who asked about om
258.hook: Satyakama asks what a life of om leads to; a, u, m hold waking, dream and deep sleep
258.carry: a, u, m: waking, dream, deep sleep
258.tomorrow: The teacher who answered with silence
258.howItsDone: Hindu teachers who follow the Mandukya instruct students to chant om as three sounds, a-u-m, followed by silence, following the Mandukya's mapping of the letters to waking, dream and deep sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: turiya, the awareness under every state. After a hundred and one years, Indra learned the self is the knower behind every state.

Six seekers once came to a sage named Pippalada, firewood in hand. He told them: live here a year first, with discipline and faith. Then ask anything. One of them, Satyakama, asked what any chanting family might ask. Sir, if someone meditates on om all their life, to the very end, where does it lead? Pippalada said: om is Brahman, both the higher and the lower. Hold one part of it, and you go part of the way. Hold all three of its sounds together, and you reach the highest.
screen: `A YEAR BEFORE A QUESTION.` → `WHERE DOES OM LEAD?` → `ALL THREE SOUNDS TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Three sounds? The Mandukya spells them out. Verse eight: this self, as a syllable, is om. The quarters are the letters, and the letters are the quarters: a, u, m. In Sanskrit the o of om is a and u blended, which is why it's also written aum. Verse nine: waking is a, the first sound, the open mouth. Verse ten: dream is u, the rounding lips, in between, the way dream sits between waking and sleep. Verse eleven: deep sleep is m, the lips closing, where the sound gathers, the way waking and dream fold into sleep each night. The text backs each link with wordplay, a sound suggesting a meaning, the kind the Upanishads use often. So say it slowly: ah, oo, mmm. Back of the throat, to the lips, closed. One breath walks through a whole day and night. And the fourth? It has no letter. That's tomorrow. This is why om comes first in so many Hindu mantras: om namah shivaya, om namo narayanaya. Before you ask for anything, you name all of it: everything you're awake to, everything you dream, everything you rest in. Some families say a quiet om before a long drive or an exam for the same reason. Today, most days are lived in pieces: the morning rush, the scrolling half-dream, the crash at night. Om is the Hindu way of holding the whole day in one breath, and offering it.
screen: `THE LETTERS ARE THE QUARTERS.` · `A WAKING, U DREAM, M SLEEP.` · `SAY IT SLOWLY: AH, OO, MMM.` · `OM COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `A, U, M.`

segments.voice: If you're comfortable, chant om slowly three times, out loud or silently, feeling each sound in your mouth: on the ah, think waking; on the oo, dream; on the mmm, deep sleep. After the third, stay in the silence and add nothing. If chanting isn't your practice, simply breathe in three parts and rest after each out-breath.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Om, letter by letter: a is waking, u is dream, m is deep sleep. The fourth has no letter.
Your line: a, u, m: waking, dream, deep sleep. A whole day and night in one syllable. That's day two hundred fifty-eight.

259.title: The teacher who answered with silence
259.hook: Bahva answers with silence; the fourth has no letter, and the week in one breath
259.carry: the silence after om is the fourth
259.howItsDone: Hindu practitioners who chant om are often taught to rest in the silence after the syllable, which the Mandukya's twelfth verse identifies with the fourth, the self beyond waking, dream and deep sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Upanishad: om, letter by letter. A is waking, u is dream, m is deep sleep. And turiya: the awareness under every state has no letter.

A student named Bashkali once asked his teacher, Bahva: sir, teach me Brahman. Bahva said nothing. Bashkali asked again. Silence. A third time: please, teach me. And Bahva said: I am teaching you. You don't understand. This self is silence. Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita, tells this story. And the Mandukya's last verse says the same thing in its own way.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `THIS SELF IS SILENCE.` → `THE MANDUKYA'S LAST VERSE.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve: the fourth is amatra, without a letter. Beyond all dealings. The world comes to rest in it. Auspicious. Not two. So om is the self. The one who knows this enters the self by the self. That's the end of the Upanishad. The fourth isn't a sound after m. It's the silence the whole syllable rises out of and falls back into. That's why teachers ask students to stay quiet after chanting om. The silence isn't the end of the practice. It's the point. It's also why some Hindus keep mauna, a vow of silence, for an hour, a day, sometimes far longer. Not to punish the tongue. To rest where words come from. And notice that last line: you enter the self by the self. Not by going somewhere else. By being what you already are. The week, in one breath. The gods hid from Death in om, which is all this. Indra looked in the water and turned back: the self isn't the body. The dreamer still weeps. Deep sleep is bliss that wants nothing. After a hundred and one years, the knower behind it all: the fourth. A, u, m, and the silence with no letter. Today, a life barely has a rest in it: alerts, noise, a podcast for every walk. Hindu practice keeps a place for silence on purpose, because many teachers say that's where the self is closest. Next, three weeks on three paths: action, devotion and knowledge.
screen: `THE FOURTH HAS NO LETTER.` · `THE SILENCE AFTER OM.` · `MAUNA: A VOW OF SILENCE.` · `THE WEEK, IN ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `AMATRA.`

segments.voice: Breathe out slowly, all the way, and at the bottom of the out-breath, before the next one begins, rest in the small pause that nobody made. Let the in-breath come by itself, and each time the breath empties, meet the pause again, not stretching it, just noticing it; if a thought arrives, let it fade the way a sound does. If you'd like, chant om once at the start and let it fall into that same pause.
The Mandukya Upanishad. Twelve verses: om is all this; the self has four quarters; a, u, m for three of them, and silence for the fourth.
